article_text:
「阪神」を超えるマグニチュード７・８

大河ドラマ「豊臣兄弟！」の第40回は天正13年（1585）、全面戦争の一歩手前の状況にまで陥った豊臣秀吉（池松壮亮さん）と徳川家康（松下洸平さん）が、和解に至るまでの過程が描かれました。

両雄の武力行使を押しとどめた大きな要因は天正地震。天正13年11月29日の夜中23時ごろに発生した歴史的な大地震です。マグニチュードは推定７・8。有史に残る日本の内陸地震としては、7000人を超える犠牲者を出した1891年（明治24）の濃尾地震（マグニチュード8・０）以前に発生した中で最大級のものでした。ちなみに1995年1月17日の阪神・淡路大震災がマグニチュード７・３です。いかに大規模な地震だったか想像に余りあります。

城が消え、利家弟や一豊娘が死亡、三十三間堂の仏様も…

被害は現在の富山県から岐阜県、三重県、滋賀県など中部地方から近畿地方にかけた広い範囲で発生。被災地は豊臣勢の支配領域とほぼ重なり、豊臣兄弟は重大な事態に直面しました。三河（愛知県東部）でも岡崎城が損壊するなど徳川側の被害も大きいものでした。

文献が限られており、すべてが同じ地震によるものなのかははっきりしないところがありますが、象徴的だったのは飛騨の白川郷（岐阜県）にあった帰雲城です。地震とそれに伴う大規模な山崩れによって、城はその城下町とともに大量の土砂に埋まってしまいました。城主だった内ヶ島一族は一夜にして滅亡という悲劇でした。

越中（富山県）の前田領では前田利家の弟、秀継が城主だった木舟城（高岡市）が三丈（約９㍍）も沈み、秀継は妻とともに死亡。秀吉に仕えた山内一豊が城主だった近江（滋賀県）の長浜城も建物が崩落、一豊と千代のひとり娘である与禰が下敷きになり乳母と共に息絶えました。摂津（大阪府）の堺でも倉庫が倒壊、また京では三十三間堂の全ての仏像が倒れたといいます。

大地震を生涯で２度経験した秀吉

発災時、秀吉は近江の坂本城（大津市）におり、あまりの揺れの激しさに大坂へ逃げ帰ったとされます。ドラマで触れていたとおり、対徳川戦の前線基地になるはずだった大垣城（岐阜県）も被災。領地の災害復興が長期にわたったことは確実で、両軍とも戦争どころではなくなりました。

なお秀吉は11年後、畿内で大きな被害が出た1596年の慶長伏見地震も経験。この時は完成間近だった伏見城が倒壊しています。秀吉は日本史に残る有数の大地震を震源に近い場所で2度も体験したということになります。

石川数正、ナゾに包まれた出奔の「わけ」

家康を幼少期から見守り、文字通り「股肱の臣」として支えてきた石川数正（迫田孝也さん）がこのタイミングで出奔。秀吉に臣従すると誓いました。天正地震の発生の約２週間前のことでした。

数多い日本史のナゾの中でも、とりわけ話題にされることの多い数正のこの行動。「秀吉に勧誘された」「徳川家内で孤立した」など様々な見方がありますが、決定的な史料はなく真相は分かりません。

家康と共に歩んだ数正の半生

「豊臣兄弟！」の中でも、家康と数正の関係は丁寧に描かれてきただけに、そうなると分かっていても出奔の衝撃は大きいものでした。

今川家の人質になった時代から家康に仕え、当主の息子、今川氏真らにいじめられる厳しい境遇に共に耐えました。

今川義元（大鶴義丹さん）に大切に育ててきた小鳥を殺され、絶対的な主従関係を見せつけられるという印象的なエピソードもありました。

この時の数正の言葉は名台詞として話題に。「奪われたくなければ奪う側になるしかありません。従うのが嫌なら従わさせねばなりません。いつの日か、あなた様が武家の頂に立つのです」と励まし、2人の間では「天下取り」が密かな目標となったのでした。

武田勢に大敗を喫し、家康の生涯でも最大級のピンチに立たされた三方ヶ原の戦い（1573年）では、数正に「おれはすぐに忘れる。その代わりお前は忘れるでない、この先、わしが同じ失態を繰り返さぬよう、にらみを利かせてくれ。諫めてくれ」と伝えました。それほど数正を信頼していた家康でした。

徳川を守るため徳川を離れた

ドラマでは、出奔の理由を問われた数正は「徳川に愛想が尽きた。いくら情理を説いても、家康も家臣も勝ち目のない戦に挑もうとしている。一緒にいたらいくつ命があっても足りない」と語り、表向きは自分と一族の身を守るために徳川を離れた、と説明しました。

しかし交渉相手として長く数正とやり取りしてきた秀長（仲野太賀さん）には、数正の真意は容易に想像ができるものでした。

「やはり徳川を守るために徳川を捨ててこられたのですね」。同じように“支える”ことに半生を捧げてきた秀長からこう言われては、数正もウソはつけません。「私もあなた様のようにいつまでも殿をおそばでお支えしとうございました」。主君の家康に無益な戦いを諦めさせるために身を捨てた数正でした。

数正の出奔を知り、哄笑する家康の姿には鬼気迫るものがありました。最も信頼する家臣を追い詰めてしまった己の愚かさをあざ笑うようにも聞こえました。

結果的に戦争を回避したことで、のちの家康に大きなチャンスが巡ってくることになりました。「秀吉も秀長も早く死んでくれないか」という切なる願望も、意外に早く「現実」のものになるとは、家康も予想していなかったでしょう。

あさひ、豊臣の天下一統の直前に…

和睦に応じることにした家康。しかし合意にあたっては「秀吉の身内を正妻にほしい」とハードルは上げました。実質的には妹のあさひ（倉沢杏菜さん）をよこせ、と要求したに等しいものです。被災で背に腹は代えられない豊臣家の弱みに乗じ、徳川家の安全を担保するに相応しい存在を求めたということでしょう。

あさひの夫の副田吉成（前原瑞樹さん）を巡っては、ドラマのように家康との婚姻のために離縁させられたと言われていますが、実際は以前に失態があって離縁させられており、もともとあさひは独り身だったという見方もあります。

ドラマでは互いに思いあう夫婦として、しかし「豊臣」という今や何物にも比べようのない「家」のため、そして世の平穏のために、辛いながらも納得して別れを選ぶ姿が印象的でした。これも戦国の世の常の風景だったことでしょう。

家康は間もなく本拠地を駿府に移し、正妻に収まったあさひは「駿河御前」と呼ばれました。家康45歳、あさひ44歳でした。

母の見舞いなどで京と駿府を行き来しますが、本人も病気がちになり、結局、京の聚楽第で天正18年（1590）1月に亡くなります。小田原攻めが本格的に始まった時期で、夫の家康も豊臣軍の中核として小田原攻めに参加しました。豊臣と徳川を結ぶかすがいとして、大きな役割を果たした生涯でした。

article_text:
Amazon MGM Studios is revamping its film division, with Julie Rapaport and Alana Mayo each being tapped as as Head of Film, Production & Development.

Both will report to Courtenay Valenti , Head of Film, Streaming and Theatrical at Amazon MGM. Valenti revealed the restructuring Tuesday and sent a note to staff.

“Julie and Alana will each oversee approximately half of our film slate — spanning all genres across theatrical and streaming — with each managing roughly 15 films per year,” she wrote. “It’s important to note that we are not creating separate pods or siloed teams, as our senior production & development team members will all work with both Julie and Alana across the entire slate, regardless of specific reporting lines.”

Read her full memo below.

Valenti said Mayo will continue continue to lead Orion Pictures, which she has overseen since 2020. Rapaport has been with Amazon since 2015 and most recently was had the title of Head of Film, Production & Development.

Here is the memo.

Hi team, I am excited to share an important evolution of our Amazon MGM Film Studio. Our output now spans more than 30 films a year across theatrical and streaming — growth that reflects the trust our studio has built with the creative community and the extraordinary work of our team. To match that scale and drive even greater creative output, I am pleased to announce that Julie Rapaport and Alana Mayo will each serve as Head of Film, Production & Development, reporting to me. Julie and Alana will each oversee approximately half of our film slate — spanning all genres across theatrical and streaming — with each managing roughly 15 films per year. It’s important to note that we are not creating separate pods or siloed teams, as our senior production & development team members will all work with both Julie and Alana across the entire slate, regardless of specific reporting lines. Julie and Alana will also partner closely with marketing, content strategy, finance, public relations, theatrical distribution and Prime Video programming to align creative, business, and financial decisions across the film team. Physical production, business affairs, casting, consumer insights, studio operations, music, and worldwide theatrical distribution will continue reporting to me, alongside Julie and Alana. We remain one unified creative team, committed to the storytelling and creative partnerships that define this studio. Julie has been instrumental in building our creative development team since she joined Amazon in 2015. Over the past decade, she has shaped a slate that includes Road House, Saltburn, Project Hail Mary , and Verity — cultivating a pipeline that consistently attracts top talent and bold material. Her creative instincts are exceptional, and the trust she has earned across the creative community is a testament to her leadership. Alongside her expanded role, Alana will continue to lead Orion Pictures, which she has overseen since 2020. Under her leadership, Orion has built beautifully on its legacy of bold, distinctive filmmaking — Oscar-winning Women Talking and American Fiction , Oscar-nominated Nickel Boys , breakout hit Bottoms , Nia DaCosta’s provocative, modern reimagining of Henrik Ibsen’s classic play, Hedda , and this year’s Is God Is and Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother . Alana has a gift for identifying and elevating bold, distinctive voices, and the relationships she has built with the talent she champions reflect the kind of creative partnership this studio stands for. I am so proud of what this team has built together, and I could not be more energized by what is ahead. Please join me in congratulating Julie and Alana. Best, Courtenay

article_text:
In an interview conducted when he was making Europa ’51 , Roberto Rossellini defined Italian neorealism as “a response to the genuine need to see men for what they are, with humility and without recourse to fabricating the exceptional.” For Rosselini, this meant building his films out of the unvarnished material of the everyday: postwar Italy’s impoverished people, and the social and spiritual problems that emerged from their lives. The title of Radu Jude’s Kontinental ’25 indicates its debt to neorealism in general, and its borrowings from the plot of Europa ’51 more specifically. This initially seems incongruous, given Jude’s reputation as one of the more satirical, hyperbolic, and media-addled of contemporary filmmakers. But Kontinental ’25 is a neorealist film, one attuned to the everyday without fabricating the exceptional—it’s just that in the present day, the everyday is pretty exceptional (and quite frequently fabricated).

Unlike that of Rossellini and his contemporaries, daily reality for Jude involves screen time, and probably too much of it. In a more subtle way than his despairingly A.I.-infected Dracula (2025), Kontinental ’25 is a case study: shot on an iPhone in 10 days, the film constantly punctures its narrative with TV broadcasts playing in the background, viral videos streaming on phones held up to the screen, and characters reading comment sections aloud. And where the aesthetic of the Italian neorealists drew from the documentary tradition, Jude’s neorealism extends to shooting raw material in a raw style, with natural light and an unmanicured mise en scène, giving his frame a flattened, open digital look that evokes the way we see the world through our devices.

Kontinental ’25 opens on Ion (Gabriel Spahiu, Dracula ’s Vlad the Impaler) picking up bottles and rubbish and muttering to himself as he walks through a wooded area that, we learn through a startling cut to an animatronic baryonyx, is, in fact, Dino Park, at the Wonderland Resort in the Transylvanian city of Cluj. Ion walks through the city, along highways dotted with presidential billboards, begging for work or money, and enduring harassment from a remote-controlled robot dog. He lives in the basement of an otherwise unoccupied building, whose absentee owner has apparently sold it to a politically well-connected company, called Europa, with plans to raze the building and erect a luxury hotel. Orsolya (Eszter Tompa), a bailiff assigned to evict the elderly alcoholic squatter, and the gendarmes who are there for backup give Ion a few minutes to gather his belongings. While they’re finishing their cigarettes, he strangles himself with a length of wire, choosing death over living in the streets.

The suicide sends Orsolya into a spiral of self-questioning and a quest for absolution, carried out in dialogues with friends, colleagues, and family. She is Jude’s version of Irene in Europa ’51 , played by Ingrid Bergman—a wealthy mother whose sudden bereavement leads her to forsake her privilege and devote herself to the poor. Through intense exchanges with leftists, priests, and other authority figures, Irene develops class consciousness and a Christian cosmology, but she also synthesizes and transcends these worldviews, with actions born of pure altruism and universal love. Europa ’51 is, by design, dialectical and didactic, pointing the way to Rossellini’s later, “educational” historical films, in which he aimed to “show the customs, prejudices, fears, aspirations, ideas, and agonies of an epoch and a place.” “Confronting a man with his time,” Rosselini maintained, “gives me enough material to construct action and incite curiosity.”

Kontinental ’25 , in contrast, extends Jude’s primary project in his narrative films: confronting a woman (it is always a woman, from 2018’s I Do Not Care If We Go Down in History as Barbarians to 2023’s Do Not Expect Too Much from the End of the World ) with her times, even as the “material” of these times—reactionary politics, propaganda, shortened attention spans, avaricious transnational capital, open sexual pathology—has become so overwhelming that the clarity of action and purity of curiosity modeled by Rossellini is likely to be swamped. Unlike Rossellini, whose characters directly confront his society, Jude’s characters speak in stories, quotations, and koans; their serious political conversations about the issues of the day digress into esoteric grievances or upsetting racist jokes. Jude gets politically incorrect kicks when people reveal their fixations in conversation—but, more to the point, he presents a world full of such unreliable narrators that it is nigh impossible for his heroines to chart a moral course through all the noise.

In previous films, Jude’s women, laboring at jobs that embedded them in the cruelty of their society, have resisted through acts of anger and absurdism. Orsolya’s anguish is more acute and self-abnegating. Her protestations of “Legally, I am not at fault” feel hollow: she’s aware of the corruption driving her city’s gentrification, but her acts of resistance go no further than off-loading winter evictions onto her colleagues. Her crisis of complicity after Ion’s suicide is answered with indifference and acquiescence from all quarters. When she unburdens herself to her husband, he looks up a news article about Ion’s death, and tells her with ironic detachment about the racist things the website’s readers are saying about her (Orsolya is ethnically Hungarian, a demonized minority in Romania); then, he tries to initiate sex. Her boss dismisses her feelings of responsibility by comparing her, with breathtakingly anti-Semitic phrasing, to Oskar Schindler. Even a priest consoles her by telling her that suicide is a sin.

Each confidante reveals their own biases. Orsolya’s mother is an Orbán supporter who relishes her own stereotypes of Romanians. A well-intentioned friend tells Orsolya a long story about an unhoused man stinking up her apartment complex, and how she found it impossible to do anything to help except call the cops, before comparing notes on which NGOs they each support. (Orsolya adds a couple Euros to her monthly phone bill for various causes—papal indulgences for a neoliberal era.) A former student (Adonis Tanța) from her days as a law professor gets her drunk, tells her funny Zen jokes about the pointlessness of existence, shows her a video of a Russian soldier dying in Ukraine, and then seduces her shamelessly.

Many of Jude’s films re-create what I’ve been told is the experience of being a woman online: an infinite scroll of harassment, reposted memes and aphorisms, atrocity videos, and the competing claims of various good causes. In the past, Jude’s women, even when flawed and abrasive, have seemed noble in their opposition to the indignities of life under capitalism, and near saintly in their endurance of sexism—so superior to their circumstances as to resemble the radical, radiant Bergman of Europa ’51 . Orsolya’s positioning is more complicated. She is the picture of liberal concern; her genuine anguish at the world’s injustices does not preclude the occasional selfish decision or tone-deaf pronouncement (she complains that her neighborhood, a new suburb, is becoming so overcrowded it’s starting to look like China), making her an intriguing evolution of Jude’s female archetype, now both victim and victimizer. The world she lives in is so gamified that posting is what passes for praxis; it makes a virtue of her outsourcing her conscience to largely symbolic gestures, like frowning with her friend at smartphone pictures of the poverty on Cluj’s outskirts, or maybe, if she’s truly serious, changing careers.

The Romania of Kontinental ’25 is being busily overwritten by the bloblike, unaccountable fixtures of international capital: Jude regularly inserts transitional shots of shoddy new high-rises, presumably built by the real-life equivalents of the “Europa” that evicted Ion, that are now springing up over Cluj’s cemeteries and around banners advertising American chain restaurants. Orsolya, who has a new apartment in one of those developments to pay for and two children to look after, sees no evident means of extricating herself from the slop of the contemporary everyday, and this darkens the tone, and dampens the spirit, of Jude’s critique. Rising out of the rubble of a war-ravaged Italy, and imbued with the utopian possibility of religious faith and political idealism, Europa ’51 is a lesson in morality. Jude’s neoliberal-era answer to neorealism is a study in nihilism.

article_text:
Joel Crawford e Januel Mercado articulam experimentação visual e intimidade em uma animação sobre preservar lembranças e continuar na vida de alguém.

É emocionante ver Jo e Raissa prometerem permanecer juntas para sempre antes de terem ideia do que isso significaria. Ao terminarem o ensino médio, a mudança de Raissa para os Estados Unidos coloca essa certeza em dúvida. A amizade continua, mas a rotina próxima e intensa que permitiu construí-la está prestes a acabar. “ A Ilha Esquecida ” se encontra nesse intervalo, representando bem esse medo de deixar de fazer parte do cotidiano de alguém e isso se tornar o começo do desaparecerimento da vida dessa pessoa.

Ambientado nas Filipinas dos anos 1990, o longa acompanha a última noite das amigas antes da mudança. A despedida toma outro rumo quando um portal transporta ambas para Nakali, uma ilha habitada pelas criaturas das histórias que ouviam durante a infância. Quando descobrem que voltar para casa pode custar a memória da própria amizade, a aventura reforça ainda mais a urgência que já estava estabelecida pela iminente separação da dupla.

Os diretores Joel Crawford e Januel Mercado, de “Gato de Botas 2: O Último Pedido” , desenvolvem a relação das protagonistas com bastante carinho e atenção aos detalhes — antes de colocá-la em perigo. A sequência que acompanha Jo e Raissa desde o primeiro encontro até o presente aproveita uma linguagem típica dos animes, e a formação da amizade se torna uma epopeia frenética. A montagem atravessa os anos com poucos diálogos, construindo a intimidade nas pequenas expressões e na maneira como as duas compartilham as situações. Quando a ilha começa a ameaçar essa história, já nos importamos o suficiente para temer o que está para ser perdido.

Esse compromisso de colocar a imagem a serviço da narrativa orienta a concepção visual de todo o filme. Ainda na cidade natal das protagonistas, proporções exageradas e cores vivas estabelecem um mundo que responde à energia das duas. A chegada a Nakali extrapola essa liberdade, com criaturas e paisagens que alteram constantemente a percepção de escala. Uma galinha pode ocupar o espaço com a imponência de um monstro, enquanto a aparição de um Cãobizomem parece perfeitamente aceitável. A opção da direção de arte é claramente recusar que o extraordinário possibilitado pelo gênero se comporte de maneira discreta.

Essa liberdade visual se aproxima daquela que “Aranhaverso” , “A Família Mitchell” , “As Tartarugas Ninja” e o próprio “Gato de Botas 2” ajudaram a consolidar na animação comercial. Crawford e Mercado exploram essa possibilidade para construir uma linguagem bastante adequada à história. O trabalho em 3D convive com passagens em 2D, sobretudo nos relatos sobre o passado, cujos estilos variam conforme o personagem da vez. Isso faz com que as lembranças também sejam novas formas de contar histórias, cada uma com uma aparência particular, em vez de receber um tratamento padrão apenas para indicar que se trata de um flashback. Em um filme sobre aquilo que as pessoas carregam consigo, essa escolha dá às memórias uma identidade que vai além de sua utilidade para explicar a trama.

A própria organização da aventura também se beneficia disso. Parte do percurso envolve reconstituir os acontecimentos que levaram as protagonistas àquela situação, no melhor estilo “Se Beber, Não Case!” . O recurso alimenta o humor e permite que novas revelações e informações incertas reorganizem o sentido de momentos anteriores, além de colocar o ato de lembrar no centro da ação. Jo e Raissa precisam recuperar o passado para decidir o próximo passo, enquanto tentam proteger uma história compartilhada que corre o risco de deixar de existir.

Nem sempre, porém, o filme administra bem a quantidade de coisas que coloca no caminho. O segundo ato acumula encontros com personagens cuja função inicial parece se limitar a apresentar uma nova excentricidade e render algumas piadas. Vários deles são divertidos, mas o tempo dedicado às apresentações enfraquece momentaneamente a urgência da fuga. É curioso que uma animação tão movimentada e frenética consiga parecer parada em certos momentos, enquanto o conflito das protagonistas espera sua vez de avançar.

A expressividade dos personagens e o contraste entre suas reações e o absurdo das situações produzem excelentes sequências, mas algumas gags insistem além do necessário, acrescentando exageros a cenas que já funcionavam. Ter um estilo com muitos estímulos não é, por si só, um problema. É que, por vezes, essa escolha acaba interrompendo uma aproximação emocional ou prolongando um encontro sem acrescentar muito ao que já havia sido estabelecido.

Essa distribuição desigual de atenção também prejudica a vilã. Sua presença salpicada pela história mantém a sensação de perigo, mas seu desenvolvimento não corresponde ao destaque que recebe na vida das protagonistas no primeiro ato, das referências em um trabalho escolar à fantasia usada pelas duas amigas. O filme não hesita em encontrar tempo para desvios cômicos e figuras passageiras, enquanto sua principal antagonista merecia um pouco mais de espaço para tornar seu conflito mais envolvente.

Quando os elementos apresentados ao longo da jornada finalmente se encontram, “A Ilha Esquecida” dá um peso emocional ainda maior à promessa que abre o filme. Perder as lembranças uma da outra significa também perder uma parte de si próprias. Apesar dos desvios, a aventura consegue transformar o medo da separação em algo igualmente íntimo e fantástico. Algumas amizades continuam fazendo parte de quem somos, mesmo quando já não fazem parte dos nossos dias.

La partecipazione della DGCC – Direzione Generale Creatività Contemporanea ad Artissima 2026 non sarà soltanto istituzionale. Tra le novità annunciate per la 33ma edizione della fiera torinese, in programma dal 30 ottobre al 1° novembre all’Oval Lingotto, c’è infatti anche la possibilità per la GNAMC – Galleria Nazionale d’Arte Moderna e Contemporanea di Roma di selezionare opere da proporre all’acquisto per arricchire la propria collezione permanente.

GNAMC, acquisizioni pubbliche ad Artissima

L’iniziativa nasce da un accordo di collaborazione siglato tra la DGCC e la GNAMC e mette in dialogo, all’interno di Artissima, il sistema del mercato e le politiche di incremento del patrimonio pubblico. La direzione del museo potrà dunque individuare tra le opere presentate dalle gallerie quelle ritenute di interesse per le proprie raccolte e proporne l’acquisizione. Un passaggio che assume particolare rilievo in una fiera come Artissima, attenta alla ricerca contemporanea e alle generazioni emergenti, e che apre alla possibilità di aggiornare la collezione museale attraverso un confronto diretto con la produzione più recente.

La presenza della GNAMC ad Artissima introduce così un elemento particolarmente significativo nel programma istituzionale della DGCC: la fiera non soltanto come spazio di promozione e internazionalizzazione ma anche come luogo nel quale il patrimonio museale pubblico può entrare in relazione con il sistema delle gallerie e con le nuove ricerche artistiche. L’accordo permette infatti alla direzione del museo di osservare direttamente l’offerta della fiera, individuando lavori potenzialmente coerenti con la storia e con gli sviluppi futuri della collezione.

Nel comunicato diffuso agli organi di stampa non è stato però specificato né l’ammontare delle risorse disponibili né il numero di opere che potranno essere acquistate.

Accanto al capitolo delle acquisizioni, la Direzione Generale Creatività Contemporanea sarà presente in fiera con uno spazio istituzionale proposto come luogo di incontro e confronto con artisti, curatori, galleristi, direttori di musei e professionisti del settore. Nel corso dei tre giorni saranno realizzati video podcast e interviste dedicate alle trasformazioni del sistema dell’arte contemporanea italiana, successivamente diffuse attraverso i canali della DGCC.

L’iniziativa coincide inoltre con il decennale di Italian Council , il programma lanciato nel 2016 e dedicato all’internazionalizzazione dell’arte italiana. Lo stand offrirà anche la possibilità di conoscere programmi, opportunità di finanziamento, pubblicazioni e ricerche sostenute dalla Direzione.

A Torino anche MIRA

Un secondo spazio sarà invece dedicato a MIRA – Mediterranean Institute for Research and Arts, il nuovo polo culturale di Messina promosso dal Ministero della Cultura attraverso la DGCC e l’Unità di Missione per la cooperazione culturale con l’Africa e il Mediterraneo allargato, insieme al Comune e all’Università di Messina e con il supporto della Fondazione MAXXI.

Durante Artissima sarà presentata la visione del nuovo istituto e, ogni giorno alle ore 17, il collettivo Polisonum proporrà in anteprima Posso sentire ciò che ancora non riesco a vedere , una performance dedicata al rapporto tra voce umana, balene e ambiente.

I talk tra internazionalizzazione e diplomazia culturale

Il programma prevede anche due appuntamenti di approfondimento. Sabato, 31 ottobre, alle 16;30, il direttore generale Creatività Contemporanea Costantino D’Orazio parteciperà al talk Open Italy: politiche culturali per l’arte italiana , dedicato alle strategie per rafforzare la presenza internazionale degli artisti italiani e, parallelamente, la capacità del Paese di attrarre curatori, collezionisti, professionisti e progetti dall’estero.

article_text:
The monograph defines how the role of the architect must change in our times

This is the first survey of Dhaka-based architecture practice URBANA’s 30-year output and 18 realised designs, which range from the Museum of Independence complex in Dhaka (completed in 2015), to Srihatta – Samdani Art Centre and Sculpture Park (opened 2025), via mosques, residential projects and corporate HQs, all of which respond to the varied contexts of Bangladesh. Plans, sketches and project descriptions are accompanied by black-and-white images by Hélène Binet. Details of soil types, settings, altitude, average annual rainfall and temperatures, and flood risks accompany each project (as well as the usual information regarding design and construction teams, and client details). It’s architecture that places the need to adapt to our changing climate front and centre: a 2005 project for the Friendship NGO in the waterways of the Brahmaputra-Jamuna River (the hydrography of which is directly affected by increased temperatures melting snow in the Himalayas) creates landforms that raise entire villages above the floodwater levels; a hospital in Shyamnagar, completed in 2018, uses harvested rainwater to establish zoning and to collect in lakes from which the local population can draw freshwater (a rise in sea levels has meant that the groundwater even 65km inland is now brackish). While you can marvel at the grace of URBANA’s architecture, as climate-change specialist Ainun Nishat notes in an essay, the work presented here also defines how the role of the architect must change in our times.

article_text:
Un museo che mette in discussione la propria storia, le scelte critiche e curatoriali, le politiche di acquisizione e, soprattutto, le narrazioni che ha contribuito a costruire e consolidare. È da questa riflessione che prende avvio il programma espositivo del MAMCO di Ginevra, che si interroga sulla possibilità di raccontare altre storie dell’arte, mettendo in discussione quelle ormai stabilizzate. Un’esigenza che trova una conferma concreta anche nei numeri: soltanto il 31% della collezione del museo è costituito da opere di artiste donne.

La questione riporta inevitabilmente agli anni Sessanta e Settanta, quando il movimento femminista cominciò a mettere radicalmente in discussione le strutture culturali e istituzionali che avevano determinato l’esclusione delle donne dalla storia dell’arte. Nel 1971 Linda Nochlin pubblicava il celebre saggio Why Have There Been No Great Women Artists? – Perché non ci sono state grandi artiste? , spostando l’attenzione dall’assenza delle donne alle condizioni storiche, sociali e istituzionali che ne avevano ostacolato la formazione e il riconoscimento. Non si trattava semplicemente di recuperare nomi dimenticati ma di interrogare i criteri stessi attraverso i quali era stata costruita la storia dell’arte.

Riscrivere la collezione

Sono domande che tornano oggi a investire il museo e che richiedono, per usare le parole del direttore del MAMCO Lionel Bovier , «Altri strumenti concettuali, altre teorie estetiche, altre narrazioni» attraverso cui rileggere artisti e artiste rimasti ai margini dei racconti dominanti.

In questa prospettiva si inserisce la doppia mostra organizzata dal MAMCO di Ginevra , in collaborazione con il Musée d’art et d’histoire della città svizzera, negli spazi del Musée Rath: da una parte Refaire collection , una rilettura della storia dell’arte attraverso opere di artiste donne; dall’altra la retrospettiva dedicata a Sylvia Sleigh (1916-2010), pittrice di origine gallese che ha sviluppato gran parte della propria ricerca a New York, dove si trasferì nel 1962 con il marito Lawrence Alloway , critico d’arte legato alla nascita della Pop Art.

Sylvia Sleigh e il rovesciamento dello sguardo

Formatasi a Londra, senza seguire un percorso accademico tradizionale, Sylvia Sleigh si afferma soprattutto tra gli anni Sessanta e Settanta con una pittura figurativa che ribalta una delle convenzioni più consolidate della storia dell’arte occidentale: quella dell’uomo artista che ritrae la donna come modello, spesso nuda e offerta – come oggetto passivo – allo sguardo preferibilmente maschile. Nei suoi dipinti sono invece gli uomini a posare, talvolta assumendo atteggiamenti e posture che richiamano l’iconografia dell’odalisca, come Imperial Nude: Paul Rosano , 1975. Ma non si tratta di corpi anonimi o idealizzati: sono persone riconoscibili, amici, artisti, intellettuali, lo stesso Lawrence Alloway, descritti con una precisione analitica, attraverso una figurazione fedele al modello, attenta alle fisionomie, ai dettagli e alla singolarità di ciascuno.

Il rovesciamento dei ruoli non riguarda dunque soltanto chi guarda e chi viene guardato ma anche il modo in cui il corpo è rappresentato: non più un nudo ideale, sottratto alla propria identità, bensì un individuo concreto, con una storia e una presenza riconoscibili.

Questa pittura così esplicita suscitò un certo scandalo nella società e nella cultura del tempo, attirando anche le critiche di chi metteva in discussione la qualità del disegno dell’artista, che appare invece forte, deciso, immediato e soprattutto consapevole della tradizione pittorica con cui si confronta. Una tradizione talvolta citata esplicitamente, come in Court of Pan (after Luca Signorelli) (1973), dove, alla sinistra di Pan, compare il ritratto di Lawrence Alloway.

L’artista nello spazio domestico

La consapevolezza del proprio ruolo di artista emerge anche nella scelta di rappresentarsi secondo una consolidata iconografia dell’autoritratto. In Working at Home (1969), Sleigh si ritrae in primo piano, accanto a una porzione di tela, nello spazio domestico in cui lavora, mentre sul fondo Lawrence è seduto a un tavolo, intento alle proprie occupazioni. L’artista riprende così la lunga tradizione dell’autoritratto del pittore davanti alla propria opera, riaffermando la propria identità professionale all’interno di un ambiente che è contemporaneamente casa e studio.

La dimensione domestica e, in particolare, quella del giardino, ritorna frequentemente nella sua pittura. In Chelsea Garden (1967), Sleigh si rappresenta insieme a Lawrence, in secondo piano, immersa nella vegetazione rigogliosa del giardino di casa, tanto fitta e lussureggiante da evocare quasi una giungla. Lo spazio privato diventa così un luogo di osservazione e rappresentazione, nel quale si intrecciano vita quotidiana, affetti e pratica artistica.

Sleigh e i movimenti femministi

Con l’emergere dei movimenti femministi all’inizio degli anni Settanta, Sleigh entra in contatto con diversi gruppi di artiste e partecipa attivamente alle loro iniziative. È coinvolta in Women in the Arts – WIA , fondato nel 1971, che promuove la mostra Women Choose Women (1973) al New York Cultural Center, e svolge un ruolo importante nel collettivo SOHO 20 . Partecipa inoltre alle attività dello spazio A.I.R. , al quale dedica il memorabile A.I.R. Group Portrait (1977-1978), ed è coinvolta nel progetto collettivo The Sister Chapel , presentato al PS1 nel 1978. La sua pittura si accompagna dunque a un impegno concreto nella costruzione di spazi di visibilità e riconoscimento per le donne artiste.

Nel catalogo della mostra compare anche un saggio inedito di Linda Nochlin , Beyond the Pleasure Principle: The Brilliant Career of Sylvia Sleigh , nel quale la storica dell’arte definisce Sleigh «Un’artista notevole e innovativa, ma non avanguardista», capace di muoversi tra «Sensualità e parodia». Nochlin sottolinea la morbidezza, l’individualità e l’atteggiamento arrendevole dei suoi nudi maschili, rappresentati con una fedeltà realistica che ne mette in evidenza la vulnerabilità, rovesciando radicalmente l’immagine di autorità e dominio tradizionalmente associata al corpo maschile. Il saggio si conclude riconoscendo a Sleigh un ruolo di primo piano nel panorama della pittura moderna.

Da Alice Neel a Jenna Gribbon: altre genealogie

Altrettanto importante, e contrappunto alla monografica di Sylvia Sleigh, è Refaire collection , la mostra collettiva che ne amplia la prospettiva storica e critica. Il percorso si apre scenograficamente oltre una tenda trasparente attraversata da scritte, mentre gli slogan combattivi delle Guerrilla Girls, su striscioni e sul pavimento, introducono alla pluralità di voci e ricerche delle artiste presenti. È una cornice particolarmente adatta alla pittura di Sleigh quella offerta da due artiste americane come Alice Neel (1900-1984), presente con il provocatorio e crudo Joe Gould (1933), un nudo frontale, scheletrico, affiancato da due figure nude e panciute, e Joan Semmel (1932), con Under the Sheet (1974), autorappresentazione ricavata da una fotografia, nella quale il corpo è osservato in soggettiva, mentre il volto rimane fuori dall’immagine.

All’autoritratto di Sleigh fa da pendant quello, assai precedente, di Louise Catherine Breslau del 1921, mentre nei corpi dipinti da Leonor Fini nel 1942 colpiscono la perfezione e la delicatezza della resa pittorica. La dimensione più esplicitamente militante del femminismo riemerge nelle fotografie di Hannah Wilke del 1981; quella della sorellanza trova invece un’espressione nel dipinto Golum (2004) di Nicole Eisenman . Fino al doppio ritratto del 2022 di Jenna Gribbon , dedicato alla moglie, che porta nel presente la riflessione sul corpo, sull’intimità e sulle relazioni affettive.

Un museo può riscrivere la storia dell’arte?

La mostra rende così evidente la possibilità di scrivere un’altra storia dell’arte, o meglio di riconsiderare quella che conosciamo attraverso opere, relazioni e genealogie rimaste a lungo in secondo piano. Si potrebbe obiettare che molte di queste artiste non sono più sconosciute e che il loro riconoscimento è ormai acquisito. Ma la questione non riguarda soltanto la visibilità individuale: riguarda il posto che queste ricerche occupano nelle collezioni, nei musei e nelle narrazioni attraverso cui continuiamo a leggere la storia dell’arte.

Parlare di riparazione sarebbe forse troppo semplice, perché nessuna mostra può correggere retroattivamente le esclusioni del passato. Il MAMCO compie tuttavia un gesto significativo: non si limita a riconoscere uno squilibrio ma mette in discussione i criteri e le gerarchie che hanno contribuito a produrlo. E soprattutto riconosce che la storia raccontata da un museo non è mai definitiva ma può essere continuamente interrogata e riscritta.

article_text:
Back in 2012, actress-turned-director Sandra Lipski wanted to crown a successful festival run for her debut short film “Going Down” with a screening in her hometown of Mallorca, but was surprised to realize the thriving island did not have its own film festival. Rather than wait for it to happen, she decided to start one herself. The result is Evolution Mallorca , celebrating its landmark 15th edition this year and taking place between Oct. 28 and Nov. 4.

Lipski was born in Germany, but moved to her family on the Spanish island as a young girl, later heading to Los Angeles to pursue a career as an actor. When the 2008 writers’ strike hit Hollywood, the actress was on the cusp of a big break. “That was very frustrating for me as an actress because that was the year I had a lot of big things coming out,” she tells Variety when recalling the origins of the festival. “I then said I would just do my own short film, which I did. Then I spent 2010 travelling to a lot of festivals.”

“I was so confused about Mallorca not having a film festival,” she adds. “Living in the U.S., there was a film festival in every tiny town, and it felt obvious to me the island would have one because it felt like the perfect festival location. I was very young at the time and just decided to try it and see what happens. I pulled some friends together, many Europeans who, like me, were born somewhere else but grew up here, and we created a very well-rounded team.”

In the years since its inception, Evolution Mallorca ballooned into a destination festival showcasing the best of cinema produced in the region but also attracting major international names. Guests who have attended previous editions include Danny DeVito, Annette Bening, Paul Haggis and Jessica Hausner. This year’s edition is set to be another glitzy one, with the festival honoring “Conclave” director Edward Berger , “Black Swan” cinematographer Matthew Libatique , “Inglourious Basterds” actress Diane Kruger , and “Triangle of Sadness” star Iris Berben.

This year’s line-up will feature over 100 projects across its program, with the festival boasting its largest feature film selection to date. International highlights include Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut,” Danny Boyle’s “Ink,” Paweł Pawlikowski’s “Fatherland,” and the opening gala in Jordan Firstman’s Cannes-dazzler “Club Kid.”

“We try having more glamorous, notable films in our international feature film section, films that have won awards from other festivals and already have a strong seal of approval,” says Lipski. “We need this section as it works as a helium balloon lifting the festival towards a wider audience. But, just a millimeter away, we are pushing the debut feature section and Made in Baleares, which is what Evolution is all about: giving a platform to and celebrating upcoming filmmakers.”

Notable films amongst the Made in Baleares section, which celebrates local cinema, include the world premiere of Juan Sut’s “Torna,” a co-production between Mexico and Mallorca following a young man who learns the house his dad left him in Mallorca is inhabited; Danna Ayelén Bosch García’s doc “Un Darrer Capfico,” exploring the intimate bond between Mallorcans and the sea; and Marga Melià’s “Putting Up With Paradise,” which revisits talks with Mallorcan artists to provide a critical, human look at the island’s past and future.

“What makes Evolution special is that these films all stand next to each other,” emphasizes the festival director. “They are all equally important to us and give the festival its soul of diversity and inclusion, reaffirming our mission of giving a platform to new voices.”

The director also says she has seen certain themes emerge in the section: overcrowded islands, housing issues for the local younger generation and finding a balance with tourism. “I don’t think it can go away; I think we just need to find a way to deal with it,” she says. “The island needs tourism as it is a main source of income, but we need to contain it so that local life is not forgotten.”

Lipski also notes the festival’s continued mission of platforming short films, which speaks directly to Evolution’s origins. “These are important filmmakers because they will be the future of the industry. And we have names like Renée Zellweger and Michael Keaton in the program, directing their first shorts. I always say: Don’t underestimate the power of a short film.”

Evolution also has a key differentiator with its Cinematography Focus, a section celebrating the art, vision, and craft of cinematography. This year’s program will be led by Cinematography Icon Awardee Matthew Libatique and delivered in collaboration with British Cinematographer and Camera & Light Magazine. Activities include a hands-on lighting workshop, an exclusive Icon Talk with Libatique, and a timely panel discussion on the female gaze in cinematography. Previous editions have welcomed and honored some of the world’s most influential cinematographers, including Ed Lachman, Erik Messerschmidt, Anthony Dod Mantle, Phedon Papamichael and Oona Menges.

Speaking about the origins of the section, Lipski says that, on the festival’s 10th anniversary, she sat down with her team – which includes her husband, cinematographer Rainer Lipski – to understand how they could celebrate the craft within Evolution. The director says there are festivals dedicated to cinematography, like Cameraimage, but she couldn’t find other film festivals with intensive programs focused on professionals. “It has really grown into a meeting point for cinematographers from all around the world,” she notes.

The festival director is also a big supporter of promoting Mallorca as a shooting destination, as well as underscoring how great a location it is to host a film festival. “In the last decade, Mallorca has really boomed in terms of production,” she says. “It’s also a sanctuary for celebrities, which is not why I do the festival here, but it’s a helpful point in showing how accessible the island is from all over the world. We are very well-connected and in a very desirable place in the south of the Mediterranean. It’s very similar climate-wise to Los Angeles, and that’s how the industry started in LA, because the climate was so perfect.”

“People just love to come,” she adds. “The island has amazing infrastructure in terms of hotels, production companies, equipment… You can find everything here. I think it’s time to give it more of a push to show that to people. We have an event called Mallorca Go, which happens on the last weekend of the festival, where we take the visiting producers and filmmakers somewhere on the island. This year we are taking them to Calvià, a municipality in the southwest that has proclaimed this year to be its year of cinema and is inviting more film shoots. We want the island to be a thriving film destination.”

Trump Administration

Utah Groups Sue Trump Administration Over Nine Mile Canyon Construction Project

The environmental organizations filed a suit against the Bureau of Land Management for approving the project that endangers centuries-old Indigenous petroglyphs.

Hyperallergic )

Months after the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) approved a road expansion proposal to expedite oil tanker truck transit through Utah's Nine Mile Canyon, three environmentalist groups have joined forces on a lawsuit to stop the project from progressing. The filing parties claim that the Duchesne County proposal will inevitably damage various Indigenous petroglyphs , historic structures, and the habitats of threatened wildlife species.

The Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance (SUWA), the Nine Mile Canyon Coalition (NMCC), and the Center for Biological Diversity (CBD) jointly filed the complaint on October 6, alleging that the Trump administration deliberately obscured and sidestepped the approval process and rejected the public's requested involvement in the decision.

The three organizations accused the BLM of failing to analyze and disclose the potential impacts of revising the existing roadway and the projected traffic increase on a cultural, environmental, and historic level. The complaint notes that the federal agency did not consult the United States Fish and Wildlife Service regarding foreseeable impacts on endangered and threatened wildlife species — including the Mexican spotted owl — and was in violation of multiple preservation and land use acts through its procedural omissions.

The BLM declined to comment on the matter, citing pending litigation.

article_text:
At Bag Factory Artists’ Studios in Johannesburg, ‘Site Forming: Where Encounter Takes Form’ brings together the practices of two emerging artists to examine memory, identity and the transformative possibilities of space.

How do the places we inhabit shape who we become? In ‘Site Forming: Where Encounter Takes Form’, artists Swaline Mkhonto and Zovuyo Pendu investigate the shifting relationships between bodies, memories, environments and inner worlds.

Presented at Bag Factory Artists’ Studios, the exhibition marks the culmination of their participation in the 2025/2026 Young Womxn Studio Bursary Award. Mkhonto’s interdisciplinary practice draws on printmaking, installation, writing and mark-making to explore fragmentation, memory and the body’s relationship with space. Pendu’s figurative paintings investigate the psychological tensions between faith, ego and the unconscious, questioning how identity is shaped through personal experience. Together, their practices approach the idea of a site as something continually transformed through encounter rather than a fixed location.

The exhibition includes curatorial contributions from Penina Chalumbira and collaboration with Letsema collective members Ntabiseng Mofokeng, Mbako Moemise and Eva Rose London. Supported by Sam Nhlengethwa, Bag Factory Artists’ Studios and the National Arts Council, the exhibition reflects the bursary’s commitment to nurturing emerging womxn artists and encouraging experimentation within Johannesburg’s contemporary art landscape.

This exhibition is on view at Bag Factory Artists’ Studios in Newtown, Johannesburg, until 6 November 2026.

article_text:
Neon has joined the release of “ NAZA ,” a documentary composed of anonymous interviews with 24 members of the Israeli military that details the country’s airstrikes on Gaza and the killing of Palestinian civilians.

The partnership marks a major sea change within the distribution market. Filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor ‘s last documentary “ No Other Land ” (co-directed with Hamdan Ballal and Basel Adra), about Israeli settler violence in Palestine’s occupied West Bank, went without a U.S. distribution partner in 2024 — a development that, at the time, Abraham said he “read it as something that’s completely political.” Many in the industry have speculated that traditional distributors had concluded that documentaries about Israel and Palestine were too controversial to do business with in the U.S. Despite being released independently, “No Other Land” ended up grossing $3.6 million in theaters worldwide and won the Oscar for best documentary feature.

For the “NAZA” release partnership, Neon will “work with the filmmakers to expand its footprint and to reach larger audiences and communities.” More exact details on how the distributor will support the film are yet to be disclosed.

After premiering at Venice Film Festival, where it was embraced by critics and won the special jury prize, “NAZA” immediately set an independent theatrical release in the U.S. and abroad. After opening in the U.S. on September 30, the film passed a $500,000 gross less than two weeks into its plan to play 85 theaters across 30 cities. The newspaper The Guardian, which produced “NAZA,” is planning to make the feature available to stream its website for free in November.

“Yuval and Rachel have created one of the best films of the year; it’s an extraordinary work of art and eyewitness testimony that stands alongside landmark documentaries like Laura Poitras’ ‘Citizenfour’ and Joshua Oppenheimer’s ‘The Act of Killing,'” reads a statement from Neon. “At the heart of Neon’s mission is a commitment to championing the best cinema from around the world. We’re proud to join the incredible team already working on the film and help bring it to the widest audience possible.”

Prior to the Neon deal, “NAZA” had already secured distribution plans across 50 countries. The film is produced by The Guardian with James Wilson’s JW Films banner, in association with Placeholder Films and Unseen Hand. “The Zone of Interest” director Jonathan Glazer is an executive producer. MK2 Films negotiated the deal with Neon.

article_text:
The Bluecoat, England’s oldest art centre, has appointed Emer Grant as its first creative director, ahead of the institution’s centenary in 2027.

Grant comes from Arts Collective, Northampton, where she’s served as CEO and artistic collector since 2020. During her tenure she presented exhibitions including Rose Finn-Kelcey and Mark Wallinger, and oversaw the £5.2 million redevelopment of the art space’s new home at 24 Guildhall Road. She has curated shows at institutions including Hessel Museum of Art and ISCP in New York, Stroom Den Haag in the Netherlands, Void Gallery in Northern Ireland and Oolite Arts in South Florida.

‘I’m looking forward to making Liverpool my home and getting to know its creative communities,’ Grant says in a statement. ‘This is a city with immense pride in its culture, people and spirit. I hope to learn from that energy, continue the Bluecoat’s tradition of presenting ambitious art, and work collaboratively to shape a vision for its next century.’

article_text:
This week, Film Comment Editor Clinton Krute is in the Czech Republic, reporting on the 60th Karlovy Vary International Film Festival. Located in a picturesque spa town, the fest has long been the home of hidden gems in its Competition sections, as well as a mid-summer stop for major films making the international circuit. This year’s edition features many of both, as well as an excellent retrospective sidebar highlighting some favorites from the festival’s past, stretching back to the days when it was located in Moscow every other year.

For our second episode from the fest, Clint welcomed critic and FC Podcast veteran Robert Daniels (RogerEbert.com) to discuss some of the highlights of the festival so far, beginning with Alain Gomis’s family epic Dao (3:09) before turning to Joan Bofill Amargós’s T he Hanging of Stuart Cornfeld (16:50), a documentary portrait of the legendary Hollywood film producer. Next, Clint shouts out Yashasvi Juyal​’s magical realist The Ink-Stained Hand and the Missing Thumb (25:42) and Robert praises Miroslav Terzić’s tense portrait of childhood bullying, 3 Weeks After (31:40).

article_text:
Japanese director Naomi Kawase has been unveiled as the head of the jury for the main international competition of the upcoming second edition of the Doha Film Festival in November.

She will be joined by French Tunisian actor Adam Bessa , Tunisian producer Dora Bouchoucha, Italian documentary filmmaker Gianfranco Rosi and award-winning Palestinian filmmaker and artist Kamal Aljafari.

The jury will decide the winning films from the 15-film line-up of international titles, from across the Arab world, Asia, Africa, Europe and the Americas.

Born and based in Nara, Japan, Cannes regular Kawase became the youngest recipient of its Caméra d’Or for her debut feature, Suzaku , before winning the Grand Prix for The Mourning Forest (2007). Her film Radiance (2017) received the Ecumenical Jury Prize at Cannes, while her latest feature, Yakushima’s Illusion (2025), premiered in competition at Locarno.

Watch on Deadline

She has previously been a guest of the Doha Film Institute , which is overseeing the festival, as one of the so-called Masters in 2016 of the body’s annual Qumra event, mentoring emerging filmmakers from Qatar and beyond.

Acto r Bessa broke out internationally in Lotfy Nathan’s Harka (2022), which earned him the Best Performance Award in the Un Certain Regard section at Cannes and Best Actor at the Red Sea International Film Festival.

He subsequently starred in Meryam Joobeur’s Who Do I Belong To (2024), which competed at the Berlinale, and Jonathan Millet’s Ghost Trail , earning further acclaim and a César nomination. In 2026, he appeared in Asghar Farhadi’s Parallel Tales . DFI supported all three of his films, Harka , Who Do I Belong To and Parallel Tales .

Bouchoucha is one of the Arab world’s most influential film producers and a longstanding advocate for emerging filmmakers. Working under the banner of her 30-year-old company Nomadis Images in 1995, her credits include Satin Rouge , Inhebbek Hedi , Weldi , Behind the Mountains , Souad and Aisha Can’t Fly Away .

Rosi is the only documentary filmmaker to have won both the Golden Lion at Venice and the Golden Bear at Berlin. His film Sacro GRA (2013) became the first documentary to win Venice’s Golden Lion, while Fire at Sea (2016), filmed on the island of Lampedusa, won the Golden Bear and the European Film Award and received an Academy Award nomination. His documentary Notturno (2020) was presented in competition at Venice, and Below the Clouds (2025) won the festival’s Special Jury Prize. He was a also DFI Qumra Master in 2018.

Aljafari is recognized for his distinctive cinematic practice exploring memory, history, identity and the politics of images. His feature A Fidai Film (2024) won the Jury Prize in the Burning Lights Competition at Visions du Réel and the Tanit d’Or at Carthage. His documentary With Hasan in Gaza (2025) received Best Artistic Achievement at Doha Film Festival. Both films were supported by DFI, which is also backing his forthcoming feature Beirut 1931 .

“Independent cinema is where the most vital, courageous and transformative stories of our time find their voice. It is our responsibility to protect the creative freedom to challenge conventions, bring overlooked perspectives to the screen and build bridges across cultures,” said Fatma Hassan Alremaihi, CEO of Doha Film Institute and Director of Doha Film Festival .

“We are immensely proud to welcome friends of the Institute who share our vision and have dedicated their lives to nurturing independent cinema. Their collective experience and artistic integrity embody the spirit of DFI and DFF: championing original voices, creating space for bold ideas and ensuring that powerful stories, find their way to audiences around the world.”

The Doha Film Festival, which expands on the DFI’s long-running family-focused festival of Ajyal which ran for more than a decade during the same period, will unfold from November 19 to 27.
